items.text: Kiran says: 'The canteen food is the best in the district.'
items.q: What kind of statement is this?
opts: A fact that can be checked
why: 'Best' is a judgement; there is no single test for it.
No study or method is mentioned.
It does not tell anyone what to do.
items.hint: Could two reasonable people disagree about 'best'?

items.text: The library is open from 9 am to 6 pm on weekdays.
items.q: What kind of statement is this?
why: Correct — you can check the timings.
Nothing is taken for granted here.
It describes the present, not the future.
items.hint: Can you check it with the notice board?

items.text: A student is always late on Mondays. A classmate says, 'They are just lazy.'
items.q: What is the classmate doing?
opts: Making an assumption about the reason
why: Laziness has not been shown — only lateness.
Correct — the reason is assumed. Buses, family duties or work could explain it.
No evidence about the reason is given.
It is a statement, not a question.
items.hint: What was observed, and what was guessed?

items.text: A message says: 'Exams postponed!!! Forward to all!' It has no link and comes from an unknown number.
items.q: What is the BEST first step?
opts: Forward it quickly to help friends
Check the official college website or notice
Believe it because of the exclamation marks
why: Forwarding unverified news can spread false information.
Correct — verify with the official source first.
Strong punctuation shows emotion, not truth.
items.hint: Where would real exam news be published?

items.text: Sam scored low in the first test. The teacher says, 'Sam will fail the course.'
items.q: What is the main weakness in the teacher's statement?
opts: It predicts a final result from just one test
why: Correct — one result is weak evidence for a long-term prediction.
Naming the student is not the reasoning problem.
items.hint: How much evidence is the prediction based on?

items.text: You find a phone in the classroom. It has a lock screen photo of its owner.
items.q: Which action shows the most responsibility?
opts: Hand it to the teacher or office and tell the class
Use it to call your friends
why: The owner may not know where to ask.
Correct — this gives the best chance of a safe return.
It may be taken by someone else.
Using someone else's phone is not right.
items.hint: What would you want someone to do if it were your phone?

items.text: The college plans to close the main gate at 8 am to reduce late-coming.
items.q: Whose perspective is MOST important to consider before deciding?
opts: Students who travel long distances by bus
why: The guard is affected, but not most.
Correct — they may be late for reasons outside their control.
Visitors are less affected by an 8 am rule.
The canteen is only indirectly affected.
items.hint: Who would be hit hardest by this rule?

items.text: Plastic waste is piling up near the college gate every evening.
items.q: Which is the most useful FIRST step towards solving this?
opts: Find out where the waste comes from and when
Ignore it; it will go away
why: Blame without information rarely solves problems.
Correct — understanding the cause guides the solution.
Anger online doesn't identify the cause.
items.hint: Before fixing a problem, what do you need to understand?

items.text: Alex argues: 'Uniforms should be compulsory because they reduce competition over clothes.'
items.q: Which is the strongest argument AGAINST Alex's view?
opts: Uniforms can be costly for some families and limit self-expression
Alex is too young to decide
why: A personal preference, not a strong reason.
Correct — it gives real reasons: cost and freedom.
Attacks the person, not the argument.
'Nobody' is an exaggeration with no evidence.
items.hint: A strong counterargument gives a reason, not just a feeling.

items.text: Robin believed online classes are always worse than offline classes. Then Robin read a study showing some students learn better online.
items.q: What is the most thoughtful response?
opts: Change to 'online classes are always better'
Revise the view: it may depend on the student and the subject
why: Swinging to the opposite extreme is also a generalisation.
Correct — update the view in proportion to the evidence.
items.hint: Good thinkers update precisely, not completely.

items.text: 'The rule was meant to help everyone. ______, students without internet could not register.'
items.q: Choose the best linking word.
why: 'Therefore' shows a result, but this is a contrast.
Correct — 'However' shows a contrast between the aim and the effect.
'For example' introduces an example of the first sentence.
'Because' gives a reason, which doesn't fit here.
items.hint: Do the two sentences agree or contrast?

items.text: Original: 'Everyone on social media spreads fake news.'
items.q: Which rewrite is the most careful and accurate?
opts: Some people on social media spread false information, sometimes without knowing.
items.hint: Look for 'some', 'many', 'often' instead of 'all' or 'never'.

items.text: A soap advertisement says: 'Eco-friendly and green!' It gives no other information.
items.q: What is missing?
opts: Specific, checkable details about why it is eco-friendly
why: Colour doesn't support an environmental claim.
Correct — vague green words need evidence (ingredients, certification, packaging).
Price is unrelated to the claim.
items.hint: What would prove the claim?

items.text: 'This video has 2 million views, so it must be true.'
items.q: What is wrong with this reasoning?
why: Correct — this is an appeal to popularity.
items.hint: Does the number of viewers tell you if it's accurate?

items.text: A class trip is planned to a place with many steps. One classmate uses crutches.
items.q: What should the organisers do first?
opts: Go ahead; the classmate can stay back
Ask the classmate what would make it possible for them to join
why: Correct — ask the person; they know their needs best.
items.hint: Who knows best what the classmate needs?

items.text: A friend sends you a funny photo of a classmate sleeping in class and asks you to post it on Instagram.
items.q: What is the main concern?
opts: How many likes it will get
why: Correct — the classmate didn't agree, and it may embarrass them.
Timing doesn't change the consent issue.
items.hint: Would the classmate want this photo public?

items.text: Many students skip the morning assembly because the hall is too small and they stand outside in the sun.
items.q: What is the real problem?
opts: The space doesn't fit everyone, so attending is uncomfortable
The sun is too strong in Kerala
why: This assumes bad attitude without checking.
Correct — the cause is a practical constraint.
A judgement, not the cause described.
Weather is fixed; the hall size is the solvable part.
items.hint: What does the scenario say causes the skipping?

items.text: 'If you are quiet in class, you don't understand the topic.'
items.q: What assumption is hidden here?
opts: That speaking is the only sign of understanding
why: Correct — some people understand well but prefer listening.
items.hint: What does the speaker take for granted?

items.text: Claim: 'Banning plastic bags will solve plastic pollution.'
items.q: Which is the best response?
opts: Totally agree; nothing else is needed
It may help, but bottles, packaging and waste collection also matter
Bags are useful, so never ban them
why: Correct — it accepts the partial truth and adds what's missing.
items.hint: Is one action enough for a large problem?

items.text: After a debate, your team lost. A friend says the other team had better evidence.
items.q: What is the most useful reflection?
opts: What evidence did they use that we missed?
why: Correct — this question helps you improve.
items.hint: Which response helps you improve next time?

items.text: 'Many farmers lost their crops in the flood. ______, prices of vegetables rose in the market.'
items.q: Choose the best linking word.
why: Correct — the price rise is a result of crop loss.
items.hint: Is the second sentence a result of the first?

items.text: Which of these supports the claim 'The new bus route helps students'?
items.q: Choose the strongest evidence.
opts: Attendance from that area rose from 70% to 88% after the route began
why: Nice, but not evidence of benefit for attendance.
items.hint: Look for a specific, measurable change.

items.text: 'Either we build the new road, or our village will never develop.'
items.q: What reasoning problem is this?
opts: False choice — it ignores other paths to development
why: Correct — development could also come from schools, internet, health, other routes.
It's a claim about the future.
items.hint: Are there really only two options?

items.text: Source A: an anonymous blog. Source B: a district health office notice with a date and officer's name.
items.q: Which is more reliable for local health guidance, and why?
opts: B — it is official, dated and accountable
why: Correct — accountability and traceability increase reliability.
Too cynical; some sources are much more reliable.
items.hint: Which one can you trace and hold responsible?

items.text: A college gives laptops to the top 10 scorers to 'encourage everyone'.
items.q: Which assumption is most questionable?
opts: That rewarding top scorers will motivate all students, including those who need laptops most
why: Correct — students who most need laptops may not be top scorers.
items.hint: Who actually receives the laptops?

items.text: A survey finds students who eat breakfast get higher marks.
items.q: What is the most careful conclusion?
opts: Breakfast and marks are linked, but other factors (sleep, routine, family support) may explain both
why: Correct — it notes the link and possible third factors.
items.hint: Correlation or causation?

items.text: A wind farm is proposed on a hill. Some residents welcome cheap power; others worry about noise and birds.
items.q: Which statement best represents both sides fairly?
opts: The residents who complain are against progress
Both groups care about the community's future but weigh energy and local impact differently
why: Correct — it finds the shared concern beneath the disagreement.
items.hint: What do both sides have in common?

items.text: A shopkeeper gives you ₹200 extra change by mistake. It's a small shop with low income.
items.q: Which reasoning is strongest?
opts: Keep it — it was their mistake
Return it — the money belongs to them, and the loss may hurt a small business
why: Correct — it considers both duty (honesty) and consequences (harm).
Still keeps money that isn't yours.
Small amounts can matter to small businesses.
items.hint: Think about both rights and consequences.

items.text: A student from another state says the hostel menu has nothing they can eat. Others say, 'Adjust, everyone else does.'
items.q: What is the most reasonable approach?
opts: Find out the need and consider simple menu options without big extra cost
Change the entire menu to their food
Ask the student to leave the hostel
items.hint: What is the smallest change that solves the problem?

items.text: A college library has 5 copies of a key textbook for 120 students before exams.
items.q: Which solution is fairest and most practical?
opts: First come, first served for the whole term
Short-time loans (e.g. 3 hours) plus a reference copy that stays in the library
Remove the book from the list
why: Early borrowers keep the books; others never get them.
items.hint: How can more people share limited copies?

items.text: Claim: 'Students should not use AI tools at all because they stop people thinking.'
items.q: Which is the strongest counterargument?
opts: AI can support thinking when used to question and check ideas, not to replace them
why: Correct — it challenges the claim with a specific condition.
items.hint: A counterargument should target the claim's reason.

items.text: You argued that electric scooters are always better for the environment. Then you learn that electricity in your area mostly comes from coal.
items.q: How should you revise your view?
opts: Electric scooters may still reduce local air pollution, but overall benefit depends on how electricity is produced
Electric scooters are worse than everything
why: Correct — precise revision using the new information.
items.hint: Update your view without throwing it away completely.

items.text: 'Online learning is flexible. ______, it can be lonely for some students.'
items.q: Choose the best linking word.
why: Correct — it introduces a contrasting point.
Gives a reason, not a contrast.
items.hint: Is the second idea a contrast?

items.text: A company says its river is 'clean now' and shows one photo of clear water.
items.q: Why is this weak evidence?
opts: One photo can't show water quality over time; tests of chemicals and bacteria are needed
why: Correct — water can look clear and still be polluted.
items.hint: Can you see pollution in a photo?

items.text: 'This app is free, so I'm not paying anything.'
items.q: What assumption is hidden?
opts: That money is the only form of payment
why: Correct — you may pay with data, attention or privacy.
items.hint: What else could you 'pay' with?

items.text: 'If we let students choose one elective, soon they'll want to choose all their subjects, and then there will be no syllabus at all.'
items.q: What reasoning problem is this?
opts: Slippery slope — it assumes one step leads inevitably to extreme results
why: Correct — no evidence that each step must follow.
items.hint: Does each step really follow automatically?

items.text: A class representative gets a free meal coupon from the canteen owner, who wants the class to choose his canteen for an event.
items.q: What is the ethical issue?
opts: Conflict of interest — the representative's decision may be influenced by a personal benefit
why: Correct — the representative should disclose it or decline.
Personal gains can bias decisions made for a group.
items.hint: Whose interests should the representative serve?

items.text: A town's lake is filling with water hyacinth weeds every year. Removing them by hand costs a lot.
items.q: What is the most useful question to ask?
opts: Why are the weeds growing faster — is something like sewage adding nutrients?
why: Correct — addressing the cause prevents the problem.
items.hint: Treat the cause, not just the symptom.

items.text: Argument: 'Exams should be removed because they cause stress.'
items.q: Which response best tests this argument?
opts: If exams are removed, how will learning be checked fairly — and do other methods cause less stress?
why: Correct — it questions consequences and alternatives.
Tradition isn't a reason by itself.
items.hint: What would replace exams?

items.text: You thought a classmate was rude because they never greeted you. Later you learn they have difficulty hearing.
items.q: What is the best lesson?
opts: My judgement was based on an assumption; I should check before concluding
why: Puts the burden only on them.
Correct — reflection on how the judgement was formed.
items.hint: What did you assume?

items.text: Original: 'The rule is stupid and the principal is stupid.'
items.q: Which rewrite criticises the idea respectfully?
opts: The rule may not achieve its goal because many students travel by late buses.
This is the worst rule ever!!!
why: Correct — criticises the rule with a reason.
items.hint: Criticise ideas, not people.

items.text: Article: 'Experts say the new curriculum is better.' No experts are named.
items.q: What should a careful reader ask?
opts: Which experts, and what evidence did they use?
why: Correct — unnamed experts can't be checked.
Useful, but naming the evidence matters more.
items.hint: Can you check who said it?

items.text: A college installs CCTV in classrooms to reduce cheating.
items.q: Which concern represents a different, important perspective?
opts: Students and teachers may feel constantly watched, affecting trust and free discussion
why: Cost matters, but the question asks for a perspective.
Correct — privacy and trust are key concerns.
items.hint: How might people inside the classroom feel?

items.text: A factory meets all legal pollution limits but nearby residents still complain of smell and headaches.
items.q: What is the best reasoning?
opts: Legal limits may not capture all harms; the complaints deserve investigation
why: Legal and harmless are different things.
items.hint: Is 'legal' always the same as 'harmless'?

items.text: Passage: 'Since the new principal joined, results have improved by 8%. Clearly her leadership is the reason.' (That same year, the exam pattern became easier across the state.)
items.q: What is the strongest critique?
opts: A statewide change offers an alternative explanation; we'd need to compare with similar colleges
why: Correct — it identifies a confounding factor and a fair test.
items.hint: What else changed at the same time?

items.text: Two studies on screen time conflict. Study X (2,000 students, 3 years) finds small effects. Study Y (60 students, 2 weeks) finds large effects.
items.q: How should you weigh them?
opts: Trust Y — larger effects are more interesting
Give more weight to X for its larger sample and longer period, while noting Y's findings need testing
items.hint: Which study design is stronger?

items.text: A policy offers loans to students 'on equal terms: same interest rate for everyone'.
items.q: What could make 'equal terms' produce unequal outcomes?
opts: Students from poorer families may need guarantors or collateral they don't have, so fewer can access the loan
why: Correct — formal equality vs. substantive equality.
items.hint: Does everyone start from the same place?

items.text: A wildlife sanctuary is expanded, restricting a tribal community's access to forest produce they've collected for generations.
items.q: Which approach best balances perspectives?
opts: Involve the community in planning, recognise traditional rights, and design sustainable use rules together
why: May not be possible; avoids the real issue.
items.hint: Can both goals be met through participation?

items.text: A hospital app shares anonymous patient data with researchers to improve treatment. Experts note that anonymous data can sometimes be re-identified.
items.q: What is the most responsible position?
opts: Share only with safeguards: informed consent, strong anonymisation, limited access and accountability
why: Accountability shouldn't rest only with a company.
items.hint: Can you keep the benefit and reduce the risk?

items.text: Position: 'Merit-based admissions are always fair because they judge only performance.'
items.q: Which is the most sophisticated counterargument?
opts: Performance reflects both ability and unequal opportunities (coaching, schools, resources), so 'only performance' may not measure merit fairly
why: Correct — it engages with what 'performance' measures.
items.hint: What shapes performance besides ability?

items.text: You supported a ban on fishing during breeding season. A fisher tells you the ban came without income support and families are borrowing at high interest.
items.q: What is the most thoughtful revised position?
opts: Keep the ban but add income support during the ban period
why: Correct — keeps the goal, fixes the harm.
items.hint: Can you keep the goal and reduce the harm?

items.text: A panchayat has funds for either a new bridge (helps 2,000 daily commuters) or a clean-water pipeline (helps 400 households with frequent illness).
items.q: Which reasoning is strongest?
opts: Compare severity, urgency and alternatives: illness from unsafe water may be more severe, but check whether temporary options exist for either need
why: Correct — weighs severity, numbers and alternatives.
items.hint: Count people, but also weigh how serious each harm is.

items.text: 'Most successful entrepreneurs dropped out of college. So dropping out increases your chance of success.'
items.q: What is the main error?
opts: Survivorship bias — we hear about successful dropouts, not the many who struggled
why: Correct — and the claim 'most' may itself be false.
It draws a causal conclusion from a biased sample.
items.hint: Who are we NOT hearing about?

items.text: A report says air pollution 'fell 30%' in a city. It compares a lockdown month with a festival month the previous year.
items.q: What is the problem?
opts: The comparison periods are not similar, so the figure may mislead
items.hint: Are the two periods comparable?

items.text: 'Our hiring AI only uses past employee data, so it can't be biased.'
items.q: What is wrong with this assumption?
opts: Past data may reflect past biases, which the AI can learn and repeat
why: Correct — biased history produces biased patterns.
items.hint: Where did the past data come from?

items.text: A college debates whether to hold events only in English 'to be inclusive of students from all states'.
items.q: Which perspective reveals a hidden cost?
opts: Students more comfortable in regional languages may feel excluded; inclusion may require several languages or translation
why: True but doesn't reveal the cost.
Correct — one 'inclusive' choice can exclude others.
items.hint: Inclusive for whom?

items.text: Your manager asks you to write positive reviews of the company's product under fake names. 'Everyone in the industry does it.'
items.q: Which response is ethically strongest?
opts: Decline, explain it misleads customers, and suggest honest ways to gather genuine reviews
Do it but only a few
why: May be an option later, but first try a constructive refusal.
items.hint: Is there a response that is honest AND constructive?

items.text: Argument: 'Individuals can't stop climate change; only governments can.'
items.q: What is the most balanced counterargument?
opts: Systemic change matters most, but individual choices, voting and public pressure shape what governments and companies do
why: Agrees with the claim in an extreme form.
Correct — links individual and systemic action.
items.hint: How do individuals and systems influence each other?

items.text: You shared a post that later turned out to be false. A friend says, 'Just delete it; nobody will notice.'
items.q: What is the most responsible action?
opts: Post a correction where you shared it, then delete or mark it
why: Those who saw it still believe it.
Correct — corrections should travel the same path as the error.
items.hint: Who already saw the false post?

items.text: Students with disabilities rarely join sports day. The college says, 'They are welcome; nobody stops them.'
items.q: What is the most useful next step?
opts: Ask these students about barriers and add events or formats designed for wider participation
why: 'Welcome' isn't the same as 'able to participate'.
Correct — removes barriers based on the people affected.
items.hint: Is 'not stopped' the same as 'able to join'?

items.text: Which sentence best expresses a careful, evidence-aware conclusion?
items.q: Choose the best sentence.
opts: The data proves that phones destroy learning.
The data suggests that heavy night-time phone use is linked to lower marks, although other factors may contribute.
why: Correct — precise, hedged and honest about limits.
items.hint: Look for precise, hedged language.

items.text: 'Students who protested last year had lower marks. So protests harm education.'
items.q: What is the best critique?
opts: The link may be correlation; students with grievances (e.g., fee problems) may already face difficulties affecting marks
why: Correct — identifies a plausible common cause.
items.hint: Could something cause both?

items.text: A motivational speaker says, 'I wake up at 4 am and became rich. Wake up at 4 am and you will be rich too.'
items.q: What is the weakest link in this argument?
opts: One person's experience can't show that waking early causes wealth for everyone
why: Correct — a single anecdote, with many other factors.
items.hint: How much evidence supports 'you will be rich too'?

items.text: A college must cut costs. Option 1: reduce library hours. Option 2: end free transport for students from remote villages.
items.q: Which reasoning best considers fairness?
opts: Cut transport; fewer students use it
Consider who is harmed most: losing transport may stop remote students attending at all, while reduced library hours inconvenience many but exclude few
why: Correct — weighs severity and who bears the cost.
items.hint: Who loses the most?

write_prompts.text: A college decides that all clubs must meet only on Saturdays.
write_prompts.q: In 4–5 sentences: Who might be helped and who might be harmed by this rule? Give one reason for each.

write_prompts.text: A classmate says, 'People who don't post on social media have nothing interesting in their lives.'
write_prompts.q: In 4–5 sentences: What assumption is being made, and why might it be wrong?

write_prompts.text: A friend says a new energy drink 'improves memory'.
write_prompts.q: In 4–5 sentences: What evidence would you ask for before believing this?

write_prompts.text: A town plans to turn a public playground into a parking lot because of traffic problems.
write_prompts.q: In 4–5 sentences: Describe two different perspectives on this plan and one possible compromise.

write_prompts.text: Claim: 'Homework should be banned in colleges.'
write_prompts.q: In 4–5 sentences: Give the strongest argument for AND the strongest argument against this claim.

write_prompts.text: A student finds the answer key for tomorrow's internal exam left on a photocopier.
write_prompts.q: In 4–5 sentences: What should the student do, and why? Mention at least one consequence.

write_prompts.text: You strongly believe that online exams are less fair than offline exams.
write_prompts.q: In 4–5 sentences: State your reason, then say what evidence would make you change your mind.

write_prompts.text: A village's only well is drying up every summer, and families argue over turns.
write_prompts.q: In 4–5 sentences: Identify the root problem and propose a fair short-term and a long-term solution.

write_prompts.text: 'Students who sit in the front row get better marks, so the college should make everyone sit in front.'
write_prompts.q: In 4–5 sentences: Explain the reasoning problem and what a better conclusion would be.

write_prompts.text: Someone posts a classmate's phone number in a public group as a joke.
write_prompts.q: In 4–5 sentences: Why is this a problem, and what should someone in the group do?

write_prompts.text: A news headline says: 'City's new cycling lanes reduce accidents by 50%!' The article is based on two months of data.
write_prompts.q: In 4–5 sentences: Evaluate this claim. What would make it more convincing?

write_prompts.text: A company advertises: 'Our tutors are the best, because our students got the highest marks in the district.'
write_prompts.q: In 4–5 sentences: What assumptions does this advertisement make?
